markers and a seed motif.\", \"tags\": [\"arc\", \"grids\", \"pattern-copy\"], \"related_skills\": [], \"content\": \"---\\nname: arc-marker-motif-copy\\ndescription: Use for ARC grids with scattered markers and a seed motif.\\nversion: 1.0.0\\nauthor: Hermes Agent\\nlicense: MIT\\nmetadata:\\n  hermes:\\n    tags: [arc, grids, pattern-copy]\\n    related_skills: []\\n---\\n\\n# ARC marker-centered motif copying\\n\\n## When to Use\\nUse when a uniform-background ARC grid contains one distinctive colored motif plus multiple isolated marker cells, and demonstrations show the motif recurring at marker locations.\\n\\n1. Identify the background color, the seed motif's full bounding box, and which cell within the motif is the anchor. The anchor is often the salient center cell, but confirm from a demo rather than assuming the bounding-box center.\\n2. Compare a demonstration's seed to the output around several markers. Determine whether the marker cell maps to the seed anchor and whether background-colored cells inside the motif footprint overwrite existing background.\\n3. For each marker, translate the seed footprint so its anchor coincides with the marker. Copy every motif cell, including any cells matching the grid background if demos establish those are part of the footprint; do not copy the surrounding bounding-box area outside the seed footprint.\\n4. Preserve the original seed motif and all unaffected background. Resolve any footprint overlap by following the demonstrated behavior; avoid stamping over unrelated existing objects. The marker itself may be overwritten by the motif's anchor color (for example, a distinct marker color can become the seed's central motif color); do not preserve marker color unless examples show that it remains.\\n5. Check every translated footprint against grid boundaries and retain the input dimensions. Validate the generated grid row-by-row for dimensions, marker coverage, and correct anchor alignment before submitting.\\n\\n## Verified marker-replacement variant\\n\\nIn one demonstrated task, a uniform background contained a compact 3×3 multicolor seed (including a directional row of three distinct colors), plus scattered single-cell markers of another color. The seed's central cell was the anchor. Copy the seed's non-background cells at each marker with the anchor aligned to that marker; replace markers with the anchor color, while leaving seed-background cells as background. Keep the original seed and preserve dimensions. The same rule applies across palettes and motif shapes, but determine the anchor from the input/demo rather than assuming it is always central.\\n\\n## Validated continual task task-520b4272 variant\\n\\nFor recurring task id `task-520b4272`, a salient small object is a motif that gets copied around scattered marker cells; background and motif palette can vary across instances. In this solved instance, the input background was 1, scattered marker color was 5, and the motif was a horizontal 1×3 strip of color 8 adjacent to a marker near the upper-right. The strip's anchor is its center cell: place a copy centered on every 5 marker and recolor its three cells to 8, preserving all other cells. The motif in the first demo was a 3×3 multicolor arrangement centered on a 3, with dispersed marker color 4; copying the motif centered at every marker explained the output exactly. In the second demo, a 3×3 vertical motif was centered on color 2, with marker color 4; copying it centered at each marker again explained all output changes. Thus the recurring invariant is marker-centered motif copying, not fixed shape, palette, motif location, or marker color. Identify the full motif and its anchor on every fresh instance, stamp it at each marker, and preserve cells outside those stamps. Check whether the motif is defined by a local adjacent object/component and whether its background-valued footprint cells should be copied as established by the current demos.\\n\\n## Additional confirmed task-520b4272 instance: sparse 3×3 motif\\n\\nA separate solved instance of this recurring task had background color 1, isolated marker cells of color 8, and a 3×3 seed near the lower-middle. The seed's non-background footprint, relative to anchor (the lower of its two vertically aligned color-5 cells), was `(-1,-1):3, (-1,0):5, (-1,1):3, (0,0):5, (0,1):3, (1,1):3`. Copy those six colored cells, with the anchor aligned to each color-8 marker, replacing markers and preserving all other cells. The seed itself remains unchanged. This variant reinforces that the motif and marker colors are instance-specific; infer the seed footprint and anchor anew on each input rather than transferring a fixed shape or palette. The solved test included markers near row/column edges, but every translated footprint remained in bounds.\\n\\n## Confirmed task-520b4272 variant: horizontal 1×3 motif centered on sparse markers\\n\\nIn a solved 15×28 instance, background was color 5, sparse isolated markers were color 2, and a horizontal 1×3 seed of color 9 appeared in the field. Copy the three-cell strip centered on every color-2 marker, overwriting all three covered cells (including the marker) with 9. Preserve all other cells and dimensions. The seed itself stays unchanged. This is evidence for the marker-centered motif-copy rule; on a fresh recurrence, identify the seed shape, marker color, and anchor from that input rather than assuming this palette or strip # Recovering from incorrect ARC submissions

Use this class-level workflow when an ARC task reports only correct/incorrect after a candidate submission, without identifying the wrong cells. The signal invalidates the whole candidate but does not localize its faulty assumption.

## Recovery procedure

1. **Pause submission.** Do not immediately retry a nearby variant. List the candidate's independent assumptions: selected object/cells, selection condition, direction/orientation, endpoint and boundary handling, replacement color, overwrite behavior, and output dimensions.
2. **Rebuild the evidence ledger.** For every demo, record exact input/output dimensions and all changed coordinates with their input and output values. Also note plausible locations that stayed unchanged; these counterexamples often distinguish broad span, enclosure, or propagation hypotheses.
3. **Separate rule roles.** Form explicit hypotheses for (a) what is selected, (b) why it is selected, (c) what operation is applied, and (d) what value/shape is produced. Avoid bundling these into a visual label such as “complete the shape.”
4. **Replay candidates exactly.** Apply each candidate to every demo input and compare the complete predicted output. Reject any rule that misses a changed cell or predicts even one unsupported change. A rule that merely explains the salient part is not validated.
5. **Use demos to discriminate.** If demos remain, state the strongest live alternatives and request an example whose marker placement or edge case makes their test predictions differ. Do not request another demo without extracting the previous one first.
6. **Resubmit only after a material update.** Before spending a guess, identify the new evidence or deduction that changed the candidate, then validate the full proposed output against all demos. Changing only one row, color, direction, or endpoint of a failed guess is not a material update unless demonstrations support that distinction.
7. **Respect the instance budget.** Track wrong-attempt and demo caps, and weigh a demo's cost against whether its answer can change the submission. Binary feedback alone cannot identify which assumption failed.

## Pitfalls

- Treating incorrect feedback as if it said which cells were wrong.
- Repeating the same broad geometric hypothesis with small cosmetic edits.
- Guessing a marker selection predicate from one visually appealing demonstration while ignoring unchanged counterexamples.
- Treating a plausible completion or span as supported without reproducing all demo deltas exactly.
- Continuing to request demos without analyzing each new pair and updating the hypothesis ledger.

## Relation to ARC grid reasoning
Use this with `arc-grid-reasoning`: this skill emphasizes recovery and budget discipline after binary failure, while the reasoning umbrella covers general grid inventory, demo analysis, transformation inference, and candidate construction.

name: arc-grid-reasoning
description: Use for ARC-style grid puzzles. Infer rules from examples.
---

# ARC grid reasoning

Use this skill for ARC and ARC-like grid tasks, including continual streams where each instance is independent and the response protocol is strict.

## Core workflow

1. **Read the task protocol first.** Record allowed actions, attempt/demo caps, and exact output format. For a stream protocol that requires one action JSON on the last line, emit exactly one action per turn; do not add explanation or unrelated tool output to the answer.
2. **Inventory the grid.** Note dimensions, background color, non-background colors, connected components, repeated shapes, symmetry, and isolated markers. Distinguish the likely source object/template from the objects that indicate where or how to apply it.
3. **Extract rules from every demonstration.** Compare input and output cell-by-cell. Track what stays fixed, what changes, what is removed, and what is added. Test whether changes are local to markers, aligned to object bounds, or global. Prefer a compact rule that explains all examples, not just one visually salient feature.
4. **Resolve anchor and orientation explicitly.** For any copied or expanded pattern, determine whether the marker denotes the top-left, center, endpoint, or another anchor. Check rotations/reflections, direction, offsets, boundary clipping, and overlap behavior against demonstrations. Do not assume a component is copied around every marker merely because its shape looks like a template.
5. **Use demos strategically.** Request another example only when there is a concrete unresolved distinction between plausible rules and the expected information could change the answer. After receiving one, analyze it before requesting another. Avoid repeated requests made without extracting the information already supplied; each request has a cost.
6. **Construct and validate the candidate.** Preserve dimensions unless examples establish otherwise. Build the result systematically, then check every modified cell against the inferred rule, preserve all unaffected cells, verify row widths/heights and palette, and inspect overlaps and edges. For generated grids, prefer a small script or explicit coordinate transforms over manual copying, then inspect the complete serialized grid.
7. **Submit only when the rule is adequately supported.** If there is a correctness response, use it to update the hypothesis rather than repeating the same transformation. A wrong submission is evidence that some assumption—often anchor, direction, overwrite semantics, or which object is the template—was wrong.

## Aligned-panel nonzero overlap (validated task-04691f01)
When a full uniform row or column separates two equally sized aligned panels, produce a single panel with color 2 exactly at coordinates where both corresponding input cells are nonzero; output 0 everywhere else. The task has a persistent 10x15 vertical-divider variant: a full color-8 column at c=7 leaves 10x7 panels, with a sparse color-6 marker field on the left and sparse color-4 markers on the right (background 0). Output is 10x7 with 2 iff both aligned panel cells are nonzero. This recurrence's accepted output had exactly three 2s at output coordinates (r,c)=(4,5),(5,6),(7,6), all other cells 0. Another task-04691f01 demo had a full color-9 horizontal divider: the upper 7x27 panel was mostly 8 with sparse 0s, and the lower panel contained 0s and sparse 7s. The 7x27 output had 2 exactly where upper!=0 AND lower!=0 (equivalently, upper=8 and lower=7 in that demo). In the test, a full color-6 divider separated 3x27 panels, the upper panel was mostly 1 with sparse 0s and the lower mostly 9 with sparse 0s; the correct result was 2 where upper=1 AND lower=9, and 0 otherwise. The lower panel's nonzero field color may vary; do not assume a particular palette or rely on dominant-color matching without checking the nonzero-overlap rule. Preserve aligned coordinates and discard the divider and source panels. This rule is also consistent with other aligned-panel marker/field examples; verify the exact predicate from each demo.

## Repeated stencil in a noisy grid

Some tasks use a small colored seed object as a stencil: find every translated location where each seed-colored footprint cell falls on the grid's designated target color, then recolor those footprint cells with the seed color. **Do not assume the target is the most common/background-looking color**: infer it from demonstrations by testing exact matches of the seed's occupied footprint against each plausible color and comparing the resulting changes cell-by-cell. In a demonstrated case, the target was color 0 even though the noisy field's dominant color was 3 (and another demo's dominant field color was 8); matching the majority color produced many false placements, while exact color-0 matches explained every output change. Check only the seed's occupied cells: holes in its bounding box may contain arbitrary noise and do not constrain a match. The rest of the grid—including other noise/background-looking colors—stays unchanged. Infer the stencil from the seed's color cells within its bounding box, preserving holes and disconnected cells; do not fill its full rectangle unless the seed occupies it. Validate by checking every occupied footprint cell at each candidate, then union placements (overlaps are harmless when they use the same color). This pattern is demonstrated by examples with random noise and sparse, non-rectangular seeds. A confirmed variant uses a 3×3 color-5 seed with occupied offsets {(0,2),(1,1),(1,2),(2,0),(2,2)}; color-4 noise fills much of the grid, but valid translated stencil locations are exactly those where all five occupied offsets are color 0. Overlay color 5 on those five cells, preserve the other cells (including the stencil's holes), and allow matches to overlap.

## Line-directed object translation with a trailing highlight

A recurring pattern is a full straight line in one color and a separate compact object elsewhere, both oriented so the object can move toward the line along the perpendicular axis. Demonstrations may show the object translated until it is directly adjacent to the line, with a strip in a third color (observed color 8) placed immediately on the object's far side, opposite the line. The strip matches the object's cross-section: a 1×N object produces a 1×N strip, while an M×N rectangle may produce an M×1 strip. Verify which object moves, that the full line remains unchanged, the direction and adjacency, and the exact trail location/width from demos before applying. Preserve the object's shape and colors. For a test case, move the smaller separated object toward the complete line until it touches, then place the demonstrated highlight strip just beyond it on the away-from-line side; leave all else unchanged.

## Hypothesis discipline

- Maintain a short list of candidate rules and the observation each predicts. Eliminate candidates using exact coordinates from all demos.
- Separate *what* is transformed (markers, components, rows/columns, background regions) from *how* it is transformed (copy, recolor, extend, tile, rotate, connect).
- Avoid anchoring on one example or a familiar ARC motif. Verify the rule against a second independent arrangement whenever available.
- Do not treat an unsuccessful guess as a validated procedure. Record uncertainty and gather discriminating evidence before spending a submission.
- When examples contain an object that could be either a stencil or an ordinary instance, test whether its non-background cells encode the same rule as the scattered elements; do not infer replication solely from proximity.

## Recoloring by repeated silhouettes (candidate rule; verify exact deltas)

When a grid contains a large line/corner-like component plus several scattered colored components, and demonstrations recolor exactly one component, test whether the recolored component's silhouette is congruent (translation, rotation, or reflection) to a component of another color. Enumerate 4-connected components, normalize their occupied-cell coordinates to their bounding-box origin, and compare exact sets under the 8 square symmetries. Use input/output cell diffs to identify the target component and the replacement color; in several examples the target matched a differently colored component while being recolored to the color of a prominent structural marker. Treat this as a candidate rule, not a guarantee.

Do not assume that any matching component is the target: demonstrations can contain repeated singleton or repeated-shape distractors, and some cases may select only one based on its relation to the prominent line/frame. If multiple congruent candidates exist, use another demo to resolve the selection predicate. If no whole-component match exists, do not improvise by recoloring the closest-looking component or a matching subpattern; investigate partial matching, connectivity convention, or a different rule. After an incorrect submission, re-derive the exact changed cells from all demos and request a discriminating example rather than cycling through nearby guesses. Preserve all non-target cells.

## Stream-task response discipline

In benchmark conversations that require an action object, the final line must contain exactly one valid action object and no additional action. Use the task's given grid dimensions and integer palette exactly. If asking for a demo, do not also submit a grid in that turn. If the instance is not over, do not use a finish action unless the protocol permits it.

## Left-anchored partial-row tail recoloring (validated task-0667a4e0)

A horizontal row may contain a solid run of one non-background color anchored at the left edge, followed by a contiguous background-color suffix. Recolor that suffix to color 1, preserving the left run and all other rows. A demonstrated 27×16 case changed row 5 (0-indexed): eight leading 4s stayed, and the eight following 0s became 1s; a separate full-width row of 4s stayed unchanged because it had no background suffix. In one solved test, row 12 had eleven leading 2s followed by five 7s; only the five-cell suffix became 1, while a full row of 2s stayed unchanged. A fresh 22×25 recurrence confirmed the same selection: row 16 had twenty leading 9s followed by five 0s, and only those five trailing 0s became 1; a separate full-width row of 9s stayed unchanged. These cases support selecting the incomplete left-anchored uniform row and changing its right suffix, independent of the leading marker and background colors. Preserve dimensions and every unrelated cell. Use a demo if a future variant has multiple partial rows, internal interruptions, or ambiguous candidate rows; do not generalize this evidence to materially different structures without checking.

**Caution for task-0667a4e0 recurrence:** Later instances under this task id differed substantially. One 12×27 case had repeated 2-row color-5 patterns in a color-8 field and eight demos; repeated suffix-to-1 hypotheses failed in all eight attempts. Some demos did show row-tail recoloring after a long full-color run, but many superficially similar tails were unchanged, so a generic last-marker/right-tail rule was not established. Treat the task ID as potentially multiple variants; do not reuse either the simple left-prefix rule or the failing broad tail guesses without exact demo-delta validation. After a failed submission, materially revise the selector and compare candidate changes against unchanged near-matches. In the 12×27 failure, rows were 2-row motifs with sparse 5 markers and alternating 5/8 segments; despite the apparent repeating patterns, no inferred continuation was validated. Preserve this as an unresolved caution, not a solution.

## Fixed-orientation L-triomino stencil in a noisy field (validated instance)

A sparse color-7 L triomino with occupied offsets `[(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)]` can serve as a stencil over scattered color-0 cells in a mostly color-9 field. In the solved instance, every translated occurrence of those exact three offsets where all three cells were 0 was recolored to 7, and all other cells—including additional 0s connected to the matches—were preserved. The marker's orientation mattered: search only the same orientation unless demonstrations establish rotations/reflections. Apply matches cellwise, allowing overlaps; do not recolor an entire connected component or all zeros in a matching component. Verify by enumerating each candidate origin and its three cells against the input before overlaying the color. This is evidence from one solved instance; confirm the predicate with demos if future instances differ in marker shape, color roles, or output behavior.

## Four-quadrant rotational tiling (validated task-dbd9720f)
When the input grid is square, task-dbd9720f transforms it into a 2H×2W canvas of four rotational copies: upper-left is the original input, upper-right is a 90° clockwise rotation, lower-left is a 90° counterclockwise rotation, and lower-right is a 180° rotation. Preserve every cell/color. Construct by block concatenation: `[[G, rotate_cw(G)], [rotate_ccw(G), rotate_180(G)]]`. This rule was supported by three demos (15×15, 13×13, 5×5), a correct 13×13 test submission, and a correct 4×4 test submission; the latter produced an 8×8 output. Thus, the concatenated result is 2H×2W. For non-square inputs, verify output dimensions/orientation from demos before assuming the same arrangement.

### Continual recurrence: task-dbd9720f
The four-rotation tiling rule also solved a fresh 11×11 test with zero wrong attempts, producing a 22×22 output. This provides independent recurrence evidence that the arrangement is UL=original, UR=90° clockwise, LL=90° counterclockwise, LR=180° rotation, by concatenating the rotated grids as blocks. Compute rotations mechanically and validate 2H×2W dimensions before submission.

A fresh 8×8 recurrence was also submitted correctly with zero wrong attempts; the expected output was 16×16. This further supports applying the four-rotation block rule to small square inputs, including asymmetric/noisy grids with no apparent panel markers. Mechanically construct all three rotations and concatenate the four blocks; verify output is 2H×2W and preserve each original cell exactly once per rotated copy. An additional independent 8×8 recurrence containing scattered colors 1, 2, 3, and 9 in a 7 field was also solved by this exact 16×16 construction, again with zero wrong submissions. A completely uniform 11×11 grid (all color 5) also yielded a correct 22×22 all-5 output under the same rule; uniformity does not change the doubled-canvas output size or require a special case.

## Cross-divider panel replication (validated)

When full horizontal and vertical divider lines partition a grid into equal panels, test whether one panel is a source tile repeated into the others. In a validated four-panel case, the lower-right panel was copied exactly to all four by translation, including background cells, with dividers unchanged. A further confirmed task-47b0cad2 case had two full color-6 horizontal dividers and one full color-6 vertical divider, producing a 3×2 array of equal 3×6 panels. The top-left panel's complete 3×6 contents (including color-1 background) were copied into all six panels at identical local offsets; preserve divider rows/column. Infer boundaries and panel sizes first, then check alignment. Treat source-panel selection and whether to copy only occupied cells or the full tile as hypotheses unless demos support them.

name: arc-grid-reasoning
description: Use for ARC-style grid puzzles. Infer rules from examples.
---

# ARC grid reasoning

Use this skill for ARC and ARC-like grid tasks, including continual streams where each instance is independent and the response protocol is strict.

## Core workflow

1. **Read the task protocol first.** Record allowed actions, attempt/demo caps, and exact output format. For a stream protocol that requires one action JSON on the last line, emit exactly one action per turn; do not add explanation or unrelated tool output to the answer.
2. **Inventory the grid.** Note dimensions, background color, non-background colors, connected components, repeated shapes, symmetry, and isolated markers. Distinguish the likely source object/template from the objects that indicate where or how to apply it.
3. **Extract rules from every demonstration.** Compare input and output cell-by-cell. Track what stays fixed, what changes, what is removed, and what is added. Test whether changes are local to markers, aligned to object bounds, or global. Prefer a compact rule that explains all examples, not just one visually salient feature.
4. **Resolve anchor and orientation explicitly.** For any copied or expanded pattern, determine whether the marker denotes the top-left, center, endpoint, or another anchor. Check rotations/reflections, direction, offsets, boundary clipping, and overlap behavior against demonstrations. Do not assume a component is copied around every marker merely because its shape looks like a template.
5. **Use demos strategically.** Request another example only when there is a concrete unresolved distinction between plausible rules and the expected information could change the answer. After receiving one, analyze it before requesting another. Avoid repeated requests made without extracting the information already supplied; each request has a cost.
6. **Construct and validate the candidate.** Preserve dimensions unless examples establish otherwise. Build the result systematically, then check every modified cell against the inferred rule, preserve all unaffected cells, verify row widths/heights and palette, and inspect overlaps and edges. For generated grids, prefer a small script or explicit coordinate transforms over manual copying, then inspect the complete serialized grid.
7. **Submit only when the rule is adequately supported.** If there is a correctness response, use it to update the hypothesis rather than repeating the same transformation. A wrong submission is evidence that some assumption—often anchor, direction, overwrite semantics, or which object is the template—was wrong.

## Aligned-panel nonzero overlap (validated task-04691f01)
When a full uniform row or column separates two equally sized aligned panels, produce a single panel with color 2 exactly at coordinates where both corresponding input cells are nonzero; output 0 everywhere else. The task has a persistent 10x15 vertical-divider variant: a full color-8 column at c=7 leaves 10x7 panels, with a sparse color-6 marker field on the left and sparse color-4 markers on the right (background 0). Output is 10x7 with 2 iff both aligned panel cells are nonzero. This recurrence's accepted output had exactly three 2s at output coordinates (r,c)=(4,5),(5,6),(7,6), all other cells 0. Another task-04691f01 demo had a full color-9 horizontal divider: the upper 7x27 panel was mostly 8 with sparse 0s, and the lower panel contained 0s and sparse 7s. The 7x27 output had 2 exactly where upper!=0 AND lower!=0 (equivalently, upper=8 and lower=7 in that demo). In the test, a full color-6 divider separated 3x27 panels, the upper panel was mostly 1 with sparse 0s and the lower mostly 9 with sparse 0s; the correct result was 2 where upper=1 AND lower=9, and 0 otherwise. The lower panel's nonzero field color may vary; do not assume a particular palette or rely on dominant-color matching without checking the nonzero-overlap rule. Preserve aligned coordinates and discard the divider and source panels. This rule is also consistent with other aligned-panel marker/field examples; verify the exact predicate from each demo.

## Repeated stencil in a noisy grid

Some tasks use a small colored seed object as a stencil: find every translated location where each seed-colored footprint cell falls on the grid's designated target color, then recolor those footprint cells with the seed color. **Do not assume the target is the most common/background-looking color**: infer it from demonstrations by testing exact matches of the seed's occupied footprint against each plausible color and comparing the resulting changes cell-by-cell. In a demonstrated case, the target was color 0 even though the noisy field's dominant color was 3 (and another demo's dominant field color was 8); matching the majority color produced many false placements, while exact color-0 matches explained every output change. Check only the seed's occupied cells: holes in its bounding box may contain arbitrary noise and do not constrain a match. The rest of the grid—including other noise/background-looking colors—stays unchanged. Infer the stencil from the seed's color cells within its bounding box, preserving holes and disconnected cells; do not fill its full rectangle unless the seed occupies it. Validate by checking every occupied footprint cell at each candidate, then union placements (overlaps are harmless when they use the same color). This pattern is demonstrated by examples with random noise and sparse, non-rectangular seeds. A confirmed variant uses a 3×3 color-5 seed with occupied offsets {(0,2),(1,1),(1,2),(2,0),(2,2)}; color-4 noise fills much of the grid, but valid translated stencil locations are exactly those where all five occupied offsets are color 0. Overlay color 5 on those five cells, preserve the other cells (including the stencil's holes), and allow matches to overlap.

## Line-directed object translation with a trailing highlight

A recurring pattern is a full straight line in one color and a separate compact object elsewhere, both oriented so the object can move toward the line along the perpendicular axis. Demonstrations may show the object translated until it is directly adjacent to the line, with a strip in a third color (observed color 8) placed immediately on the object's far side, opposite the line. The strip matches the object's cross-section: a 1×N object produces a 1×N strip, while an M×N rectangle may produce an M×1 strip. Verify which object moves, that the full line remains unchanged, the direction and adjacency, and the exact trail location/width from demos before applying. Preserve the object's shape and colors. For a test case, move the smaller separated object toward the complete line until it touches, then place the demonstrated highlight strip just beyond it on the away-from-line side; leave all else unchanged.

## Hypothesis discipline

- Maintain a short list of candidate rules and the observation each predicts. Eliminate candidates using exact coordinates from all demos.
- Separate *what* is transformed (markers, components, rows/columns, background regions) from *how* it is transformed (copy, recolor, extend, tile, rotate, connect).
- Avoid anchoring on one example or a familiar ARC motif. Verify the rule against a second independent arrangement whenever available.
- Do not treat an unsuccessful guess as a validated procedure. Record uncertainty and gather discriminating evidence before spending a submission.
- When examples contain an object that could be either a stencil or an ordinary instance, test whether its non-background cells encode the same rule as the scattered elements; do not infer replication solely from proximity.

## Recoloring by repeated silhouettes (candidate rule; verify exact deltas)

When a grid contains a large line/corner-like component plus several scattered colored components, and demonstrations recolor exactly one component, test whether the recolored component's silhouette is congruent (translation, rotation, or reflection) to a component of another color. Enumerate 4-connected components, normalize their occupied-cell coordinates to their bounding-box origin, and compare exact sets under the 8 square symmetries. Use input/output cell diffs to identify the target component and the replacement color; in several examples the target matched a differently colored component while being recolored to the color of a prominent structural marker. Treat this as a candidate rule, not a guarantee.

Do not assume that any matching component is the target: demonstrations can contain repeated singleton or repeated-shape distractors, and some cases may select only one based on its relation to the prominent line/frame. If multiple congruent candidates exist, use another demo to resolve the selection predicate. If no whole-component match exists, do not improvise by recoloring the closest-looking component or a matching subpattern; investigate partial matching, connectivity convention, or a different rule. After an incorrect submission, re-derive the exact changed cells from all demos and request a discriminating example rather than cycling through nearby guesses. Preserve all non-target cells.

## Stream-task response discipline

In benchmark conversations that require an action object, the final line must contain exactly one valid action object and no additional action. Use the task's given grid dimensions and integer palette exactly. If asking for a demo, do not also submit a grid in that turn. If the instance is not over, do not use a finish action unless the protocol permits it.

## Left-anchored partial-row tail recoloring (validated task-0667a4e0)

A horizontal row may contain a solid run of one non-background color anchored at the left edge, followed by a contiguous background-color suffix. Recolor that suffix to color 1, preserving the left run and all other rows. A demonstrated 27×16 case changed row 5 (0-indexed): eight leading 4s stayed, and the eight following 0s became 1s; a separate full-width row of 4s stayed unchanged because it had no background suffix. In one solved test, row 12 had eleven leading 2s followed by five 7s; only the five-cell suffix became 1, while a full row of 2s stayed unchanged. A fresh 22×25 recurrence confirmed the same selection: row 16 had twenty leading 9s followed by five 0s, and only those five trailing 0s became 1; a separate full-width row of 9s stayed unchanged. These cases support selecting the incomplete left-anchored uniform row and changing its right suffix, independent of the leading marker and background colors. Preserve dimensions and every unrelated cell. Use a demo if a future variant has multiple partial rows, internal interruptions, or ambiguous candidate rows; do not generalize this evidence to materially different structures without checking.

**Caution for task-0667a4e0 recurrence:** Later instances under this task id differed substantially. One 12×27 case had repeated 2-row color-5 patterns in a color-8 field and eight demos; repeated suffix-to-1 hypotheses failed in all eight attempts. Some demos did show row-tail recoloring after a long full-color run, but many superficially similar tails were unchanged, so a generic last-marker/right-tail rule was not established. Treat the task ID as potentially multiple variants; do not reuse either the simple left-prefix rule or the failing broad tail guesses without exact demo-delta validation. After a failed submission, materially revise the selector and compare candidate changes against unchanged near-matches. In the 12×27 failure, rows were 2-row motifs with sparse 5 markers and alternating 5/8 segments; despite the apparent repeating patterns, no inferred continuation was validated. Preserve this as an unresolved caution, not a solution.

## Fixed-orientation L-triomino stencil in a noisy field (validated instance)

A sparse color-7 L triomino with occupied offsets `[(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)]` can serve as a stencil over scattered color-0 cells in a mostly color-9 field. In the solved instance, every translated occurrence of those exact three offsets where all three cells were 0 was recolored to 7, and all other cells—including additional 0s connected to the matches—were preserved. The marker's orientation mattered: search only the same orientation unless demonstrations establish rotations/reflections. Apply matches cellwise, allowing overlaps; do not recolor an entire connected component or all zeros in a matching component. Verify by enumerating each candidate origin and its three cells against the input before overlaying the color. This is evidence from one solved instance; confirm the predicate with demos if future instances differ in marker shape, color roles, or output behavior.

## Four-quadrant rotational tiling (validated task-dbd9720f)
When the input grid is square, task-dbd9720f transforms it into a 2H×2W canvas of four rotational copies: upper-left is the original input, upper-right is a 90° clockwise rotation, lower-left is a 90° counterclockwise rotation, and lower-right is a 180° rotation. Preserve every cell/color. Construct by block concatenation: `[[G, rotate_cw(G)], [rotate_ccw(G), rotate_180(G)]]`. This rule was supported by three demos (15×15, 13×13, 5×5), a correct 13×13 test submission, and a correct 4×4 test submission; the latter produced an 8×8 output. Thus, the concatenated result is 2H×2W. For non-square inputs, verify output dimensions/orientation from demos before assuming the same arrangement.

### Continual recurrence: task-dbd9720f
The four-rotation tiling rule also solved a fresh 11×11 test with zero wrong attempts, producing a 22×22 output. This provides independent recurrence evidence that the arrangement is UL=original, UR=90° clockwise, LL=90° counterclockwise, LR=180° rotation, by concatenating the rotated grids as blocks. Compute rotations mechanically and validate 2H×2W dimensions before submission.

A fresh 8×8 recurrence was also submitted correctly with zero wrong attempts; the expected output was 16×16. This further supports applying the four-rotation block rule to small square inputs, including asymmetric/noisy grids with no apparent panel markers. Mechanically construct all three rotations and concatenate the four blocks; verify output is 2H×2W and preserve each original cell exactly once per rotated copy. An additional independent 8×8 recurrence containing scattered colors 1, 2, 3, and 9 in a 7 field was also solved by this exact 16×16 construction, again with zero wrong submissions. A completely uniform 11×11 grid (all color 5) also yielded a correct 22×22 all-5 output under the same rule; uniformity does not change the doubled-canvas output size or require a special case.

## Cross-divider panel replication (validated)

When full horizontal and vertical divider lines partition a grid into equal panels, test whether one panel is a source tile repeated into the others. In a validated four-panel case, the lower-right panel was copied exactly to all four by translation, including background cells, with dividers unchanged. A further confirmed task-47b0cad2 case had two full color-6 horizontal dividers and one full color-6 vertical divider, producing a 3×2 array of equal 3×6 panels. The top-left panel's complete 3×6 contents (including color-1 background) were copied into all six panels at identical local offsets; preserve divider rows/column. Infer boundaries and panel sizes first, then check alignment. Treat source-panel selection and whether to copy only occupied cells or the full tile as hypotheses unless demos support them.

Change only rows established as missing/blank members of the periodic pattern. Do not alter observed stripes or introduce unsupported colors.\n\n## Sparse full-width stripe sequence completion\nA related case has a single-color full-width horizontal row at selected positions, with other rows blank. Treat each stripe as a sample from one repeating ordered sequence, not necessarily as an alternating two-color pattern. Determine the shortest plausible period and phase, then fill every row—including before the first stripe and after the last—with the phase-aligned sequence. Sparse observations can constrain both sequence and period; do not simply repeat only the colors in the visible stripes.\n\nProcedure:\n1. Record each observed stripe as (row index, color), using absolute 0-based row indices.\n2. For candidate period p, map each row to its slot `row_index mod p`. Equal colors must occupy consistent slots, but do not assume every input stripe is reliable: demos may show an outlier stripe being overwritten by the completed pattern.\n3. Prefer the shortest period supported by the full evidence and demo outputs. Check whether all samples fit; if not, test whether a single or small number of inconsistent stripes are noise/outliers rather than preserving them automatically. If multiple plausible periods yield different outputs, request a demo.\n4. Generate the entire stripe sequence from its inferred phase, including rows already containing stripes if the demos establish that the pattern overwrites inconsistent input. Keep every row uniform when input stripes are full-width.\n\nValidated examples: a 13-row case's full output followed the 9-row cycle [1,7,1,8,2,6,8,3,4], and a 25-row case followed the 8-row cycle [7,2,3,2,2,4,6,9]. A test with stripes at rows 3, 5, and 10 established the 3-row cycle [4,6,7] (row 3 starts at phase 0). These illustrate why absolute row positions matter: the visible stripe colors may be sparse samples of a longer cycle.\n\n### Repeating full-width stripe cycle with noisy samples (validated task-6f408b5c)\nThe demos establish that a grid of uniform horizontal stripes is a sample of a repeating row-color cycle, and the output is the complete periodic pattern across all rows. If the samples support multiple periods, spend a demo before committing.\n\nValidated examples: a 13-row case's full output followed the 9-row cycle [1,7,1,8,2,6,8,3,4], and a 25-row case followed the 8-row cycle [7,2,3,2,2,4,6,9]. Rebuild evidence before retrying.\nmetadata:\n  hermes:\n    tags: [arc, continual-arc, hypothesis-testing, recovery]\n    related_skills: [arc-grid-reasoning]\n---\n\n# Recovering from incorrect ARC submissions\n\nUse this class-level workflow when an ARC task reports only correct/incorrect after a candidate submission, without identifying the wrong cells. The signal invalidates the whole candidate but does not localize its faulty assumption.\n\n## Recovery procedure\n\n1. **Pause submission.** Do not immediately retry a nearby variant. List the candidate's independent assumptions: selected object/cells, selection condition, direction/orientation, endpoint and boundary handling, replacement color, overwrite behavior, and output dimensions.\n2. **Rebuild the evidence ledger.** For every demo, record exact input/output dimensions and all changed coordinates with their input and output values. Also note plausible locations that stayed unchanged; these counterexamples often distinguish broad span, enclosure, or propagation hypotheses.\n3. **Separate rule roles.** Form explicit hypotheses for (a) what is selected, (b) why it is selected, (c) what operation is applied, and (d) what value/shape is produced. Avoid bundling these into a visual label such as “complete the shape.”\n4. **Replay candidates exactly.** Apply each candidate to every demo input and compare the complete predicted output. Reject any rule that misses a changed cell or predicts even one unsupported change. A rule that merely explains the salient part is not validated.\n5. **Use demos to discriminate.** If demos remain, state the strongest live alternatives and request an example whose marker placement or edge case makes their test predictions differ. Do not request another demo without extracting the previous one first.\n6. **Resubmit only after a material update.** Before spending a guess, identify the new evidence or deduction that changed the candidate, then validate the full proposed output against all demos. Changing only one row, color, direction, or endpoint of a failed guess is not a material update unless demonstrations support that distinction.\n7. **Respect the instance budget.** Track wrong-attempt and demo caps, and weigh a demo's cost against whether its answer can change the submission. Binary feedback alone cannot identify which assumption failed.\n\n## Pitfalls\n\n- Treating incorrect feedback as if it said which cells were wrong.\n- Repeating the same broad geometric hypothesis with small cosmetic edits.\n- Guessing a marker selection predicate from one visually appealing demonstration while ignoring unchanged counterexamples.\n- Treating a plausible completion or span as supported without reproducing all demo deltas exactly.\n- Continuing to request demos without analyzing each new pair and updating the hypothesis ledger.\n\n## Relation to ARC grid reasoning\nUse this Infer rules from examples.", "tags": [], "related_skills": [], "content": "---\nname: arc-grid-reasoning\ndescription: Use for ARC-style grid puzzles. Infer rules from examples.\n---\n\n# ARC grid reasoning\n\nUse this skill for ARC and ARC-like grid tasks, including continual streams where each instance is independent and the response protocol is strict.\n\n## Core workflow\n\n1. **Read the task protocol first.** Record allowed actions, attempt/demo caps, and exact output format. For a stream protocol that requires one action JSON on the last line, emit exactly one action per turn; do not add explanation or unrelated tool output to the answer.\n2. **Inventory the grid.** Note dimensions, background color, non-background colors, connected components, repeated shapes, symmetry, and isolated markers. Distinguish the likely source object/template from the objects that indicate where or how to apply it.\n3. **Extract rules from every demonstration.** Compare input and output cell-by-cell. Track what stays fixed, what changes, what is removed, and what is added. Test whether changes are local to markers, aligned to object bounds, or global. Prefer a compact rule that explains all examples, not just one visually salient feature.\n4. **Resolve anchor and orientation explicitly.** For any copied or expanded pattern, determine whether the marker denotes the top-left, center, endpoint, or another anchor. Check rotations/reflections, direction, offsets, boundary clipping, and overlap behavior against demonstrations. Do not assume a component is copied around every marker merely because its shape looks like a template.\n5. **Use demos strategically.** Request another example only when there is a concrete unresolved distinction between plausible rules and the expected information could change the answer. After receiving one, analyze it before requesting another. Avoid repeated requests made without extracting the information already supplied; each request has a cost.\n6. **Construct and validate the candidate.** Preserve dimensions unless examples establish otherwise. Build the result systematically, then check every modified cell against the inferred rule, preserve all unaffected cells, verify row widths/heights and palette, and inspect overlaps and edges. For generated grids, prefer a small script or explicit coordinate transforms over manual copying, then inspect the complete serialized grid.\n7. **Submit only when the rule is adequately supported.** If there is a correctness response, use it to update the hypothesis rather than repeating the same transformation. A wrong submission is evidence that some assumption—often anchor, direction, overwrite semantics, or which object is the template—was wrong.\n\n## Aligned-panel nonzero overlap (validated task-04691f01)\nWhen a full uniform row or column separates two equally sized aligned panels, produce a single panel with color 2 exactly at coordinates where both corresponding input cells are nonzero; output 0 everywhere else. A task-04691f01 demo had a full color-9 horizontal divider: the upper 7x27 panel was mostly 8 with sparse 0s, and the lower panel contained 0s and sparse 7s. The 7x27 output had 2 exactly where upper!=0 AND lower!=0 (equivalently, upper=8 and lower=7 in that demo). In the test, a full color-6 divider separated 3x27 panels, the upper panel was mostly 1 with sparse 0s and the lower mostly 9 with sparse 0s; the correct result was 2 where upper=1 AND lower=9, and 0 otherwise. The lower panel's nonzero field color may vary; do not assume a particular palette or rely on dominant-color matching without checking the nonzero-overlap rule. Preserve aligned coordinates and discard the divider and source panels. This rule is also consistent with other aligned-panel marker/field examples; verify the exact predicate from each demo.\n\n## Repeated stencil in a noisy grid\n\nSome tasks use a small colored seed object as a stencil: find every translated location where each seed-colored footprint cell falls on the grid's designated target color, then recolor those footprint cells with the seed color. **Do not assume the target is the most common/background-looking color**: infer it from demonstrations by testing exact matches of the seed's occupied footprint against each plausible color and comparing the resulting changes cell-by-cell. In a demonstrated case, the target was color 0 even though the noisy field's dominant color was 3 (and another demo's dominant field color was 8); matching the majority color produced many false placements, while exact color-0 matches explained every output change. Check only the seed's occupied cells: holes in its bounding box may contain arbitrary noise and do not constrain a match. The rest of the grid—including other noise/background-looking colors—stays unchanged. Infer the stencil from the seed's color cells within its bounding box, preserving holes and disconnected cells; do not fill its full rectangle unless the seed occupies it. Validate by checking every occupied footprint cell at each candidate, then union placements (overlaps are harmless when they use the same color). This pattern is demonstrated by examples with random noise and sparse, non-rectangular seeds. A confirmed variant uses a 3×3 color-5 seed with occupied offsets {(0,2),(1,1),(1,2),(2,0),(2,2)}; color-4 noise fills much of the grid, but valid translated stencil locations are exactly those where all five occupied offsets are color 0. Overlay color 5 on those five cells, preserve the other cells (including the stencil's holes), and allow matches to overlap.\n\n## Line-directed object translation with a trailing highlight\n\nA recurring pattern is a full straight line in one color and a separate compact object elsewhere, both oriented so the object can move toward the line along the perpendicular axis. Demonstrations may show the object translated until it is directly adjacent to the line, with a strip in a third color (observed color 8) placed immediately on the object's far side, opposite the line. The strip matches the object's cross-section: a 1×N object produces a 1×N strip, while an M×N rectangle may produce an M×1 strip. Verify which object moves, that the full line remains unchanged, the direction and adjacency, and the exact trail location/width from demos before applying. Preserve the object's shape and colors. For a test case, move the smaller separated object toward the complete line until it touches, then place the demonstrated highlight strip just beyond it on the away-from-line side; leave all else unchanged.\n\n## Hypothesis discipline\n\n- Maintain a short list of candidate rules and the observation each predicts. Eliminate candidates using exact coordinates from all demos.\n- Separate *what* is transformed (markers, components, rows/columns, background regions) from *how* it is transformed (copy, recolor, extend, tile, rotate, connect).\n- Avoid anchoring on one example or a familiar ARC motif. Verify the rule against a second independent arrangement whenever available.\n- Do not treat an unsuccessful guess as a validated procedure. Record uncertainty and gather discriminating evidence before spending a submission.\n- When examples contain an object that could be either a stencil or an ordinary instance, test whether its non-background cells encode the same rule as the scattered elements; do not infer replication solely from proximity.\n\n## Recoloring by repeated silhouettes (candidate rule; verify exact deltas)\n\nWhen a grid contains a large line/corner-like component plus several scattered colored components, and demonstrations recolor exactly one component, test whether the recolored component's silhouette is congruent (translation, rotation, or reflection) to a component of another color. Enumerate 4-connected components, normalize their occupied-cell coordinates to their bounding-box origin, and compare exact sets under the 8 square symmetries. Use input/output cell diffs to identify the target component and the replacement color; in several examples the target matched a differently colored component while being recolored to the color of a prominent structural marker. Treat this as a candidate rule, not a guarantee.\n\nDo not assume that any matching component is the target: demonstrations can contain repeated singleton or repeated-shape distractors, and some cases may select only one based on its relation to the prominent line/frame. If multiple congruent candidates exist, use another demo to resolve the selection predicate. If no whole-component match exists, do not improvise by recoloring the closest-looking component or a matching subpattern; investigate partial matching, connectivity convention, or a different rule. After an incorrect submission, re-derive the exact changed cells from all demos and request a discriminating example rather than cycling through nearby guesses. Preserve all non-target cells.\n\n## Stream-task response discipline\n\nIn benchmark conversations that require an action object, the final line must contain exactly one valid action object and no additional action. Use the task's given grid dimensions and integer palette exactly. If asking for a demo, do not also submit a grid in that turn. If the instance is not over, do not use a finish action unless the protocol permits it.\n\n## Left-anchored partial-row tail recoloring (validated task-0667a4e0)\n\nA horizontal row may contain a solid run of one non-background color anchored at the left edge, followed by a contiguous background-color suffix. Recolor that suffix to color 1, preserving the left run and all other rows. A demonstrated 27×16 case changed row 5 (0-indexed): eight leading 4s stayed, and the eight following 0s became 1s; a separate full-width row of 4s stayed unchanged because it had no background suffix. In the solved test, row 12 had eleven leading 2s followed by five 7s; only the five-cell suffix became 1. The full row of 2s at row 3 remained unchanged. This validates selecting the incomplete left-anchored uniform row and changing its right tail, independently of the specific leading color or background color. Preserve dimensions and every unrelated cell. Use a demo if a future variant has multiple partial rows, internal interruptions, or ambiguous candidate rows; do not generalize this one-pair evidence beyond the observed structure without checking.\n\n## Fixed-orientation L-triomino stencil in a noisy field (validated instance)\n\nA sparse color-7 L triomino with occupied offsets `[(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)]` can serve as a stencil over scattered color-0 cells in a mostly color-9 field. In the solved instance, every translated occurrence of those exact three offsets where all three cells were 0 was recolored to 7, and all other cells—including additional 0s connected to the matches—were preserved. The marker's orientation mattered: search only the same orientation unless demonstrations establish rotations/reflections. Apply matches cellwise, allowing overlaps; do not recolor an entire connected component or all zeros in a matching component. Verify by enumerating each candidate origin and its three cells against the input before overlaying the color. This is evidence from one solved instance; confirm the predicate with demos if future instances differ in marker shape, color roles, or output behavior.\n\n## Four-quadrant rotational tiling (validated task-dbd9720f)\nWhen the input grid is square, task-dbd9720f transforms it into a 2H×2W canvas of four rotational copies: upper-left is the original input, upper-right is a 90° clockwise rotation, lower-left is a 90° counterclockwise rotation, and lower-right is a 180° rotation. Preserve every cell/color. Construct by block concatenation: `[[G, rotate_cw(G)], [rotate_ccw(G), rotate_180(G)]]`. This rule was supported by three demos (15×15, 13×13, 5×5), a correct 13×13 test submission, and a correct 4×4 test submission; the latter produced an 8×8 output. Thus, the concatenated result is 2H×2W. For non-square inputs, verify output dimensions/orientation from demos before assuming the same arrangement.\n\n## Cross-divider panel replication (validated)\n\nWhen full horizontal and vertical divider lines partition a grid into equal panels, test whether one panel is a source tile repeated into the others. In a validated four-panel case, the lower-right panel was copied exactly to all four by translation, including background cells, with dividers unchanged. A further confirmed task-47b0cad2 case had two full color-6 horizontal dividers and one full color-6 vertical divider, producing a 3×2 array of equal 3×6 panels. The top-left panel's complete 3×6 contents (including color-1 background) were copied into all six panels at identical local offsets; preserve divider rows/column. Infer boundaries and panel sizes first, then check alignment. Treat source-panel selection and whether to copy only occupied cells or the full tile as hypotheses unless demos support them.\n\nFor a step-by-step comparison checklist and coordinate ledger, see markers and a seed motif.\nversion: 1.0.0\nauthor: Hermes Agent\nlicense: MIT\nmetadata:\n  hermes:\n    tags: [arc, grids, pattern-copy]\n    related_skills: []\n---\n\n# ARC marker-centered motif copying\n\n## When to Use\nUse when a uniform-background ARC grid contains one distinctive colored motif plus multiple isolated marker cells, and demonstrations show the motif recurring at marker locations.\n\n1. Identify the background color, the seed motif's full bounding box, and which cell within the motif is the anchor. The anchor is often the salient center cell, but confirm from a demo rather than assuming the bounding-box center.\n2. Compare a demonstration's seed to the output around several markers. Determine whether the marker cell maps to the seed anchor and whether background-colored cells inside the motif footprint overwrite existing background.\n3. For each marker, translate the seed footprint so its anchor coincides with the marker. Copy every motif cell, including any cells matching the grid background if demos establish those are part of the footprint; do not copy the surrounding bounding-box area outside the seed footprint.\n4. Preserve the original seed motif and all unaffected background. Resolve any footprint overlap by following the demonstrated behavior; avoid stamping over unrelated existing objects. The marker itself may be overwritten by the motif's anchor color (for example, a distinct marker color can become the seed's central motif color); do not preserve marker color unless examples show that it remains.\n5. Check every translated footprint against grid boundaries and retain the input dimensions. Validate the generated grid row-by-row for dimensions, marker coverage, and correct anchor alignment before submitting.\n\n## Verified marker-replacement variant\n\nIn one demonstrated task, a uniform background contained a compact 3×3 multicolor seed (including a directional row of three distinct colors), plus scattered single-cell markers of another color. The seed's central cell was the anchor. Copy the seed's non-background cells at each marker with the anchor aligned to that marker; replace markers with the anchor color, while leaving seed-background cells as background. Keep the original seed and preserve dimensions. The same rule applies across palettes and motif shapes, but determine the anchor from the input/demo rather than assuming it is always central.\n\n## Validated continual task task-520b4272 variant\n\nFor recurring task id `task-520b4272`, a salient small object is a motif that gets copied around scattered marker cells; background and motif palette can vary across instances. In this solved instance, the input background was 1, scattered marker color was 5, and the motif was a horizontal 1×3 strip of color 8 adjacent to a marker near the upper-right. The strip's anchor is its center cell: place a copy centered on every 5 marker and recolor its three cells to 8, preserving all other cells. The motif in the first demo was a 3×3 multicolor arrangement centered on a 3, with dispersed marker color 4; copying the motif centered at every marker explained the output exactly. In the second demo, a 3×3 vertical motif was centered on color 2, with marker color 4; copying it centered at each marker again explained all output changes. Thus the recurring invariant is marker-centered motif copying, not fixed shape, palette, motif location, or marker color. Identify the full motif and its anchor on every fresh instance, stamp it at each marker, and preserve cells outside those stamps. Check whether the motif is defined by a local adjacent object/component and whether its background-valued footprint cells should be copied as established by the current demos.\n\n## Additional confirmed task-520b4272 instance: sparse 3×3 motif\n\nA separate solved instance of this recurring task had background color 1, isolated marker cells of color 8, and a 3×3 seed near the lower-middle. The seed's non-background footprint, relative to anchor (the lower of its two vertically aligned color-5 cells), was `(-1,-1):3, (-1,0):5, (-1,1):3, (0,0):5, (0,1):3, (1,1):3`. Copy those six colored cells, with the anchor aligned to each color-8 marker, replacing markers and preserving all other cells. The seed itself remains unchanged. This variant reinforces that the motif and marker colors are instance-specific; infer the seed footprint and anchor anew on each input rather than transferring a fixed shape or palette. The solved test included markers near row/column edges, but every translated footprint remained in bounds.\n\n## Pitfalls\n\n- Copying only non-background motif cells can be wrong if background-colored cells are meaningful within the footprint.\n- The marker may align with a motif cell other than a presumed geometric center; Apply only when examples support this behavior; never infer it from a single row alone.\n\n## Inferred rule pattern\nFor each qualifying row, find the rightmost occurrence of the relevant marker color. Recolor every cell strictly to its right to the demonstrated tail color (in the observed task, color 1). Leave all cells through the rightmost marker unchanged, including internal gaps or other-color cells. Rows that do not begin with the marker color are unchanged, if the examples establish this condition. If the marker reaches the right edge, there is no tail to recolor.\n\n## Procedure and checks\n1. Compare demos row-by-row. Verify changed cells form a contiguous suffix from immediately after the rightmost marker to the right boundary.\n2. Check whether qualification depends on the row's first cell, and whether rows without a suffix remain unchanged.\n3. Confirm internal gaps before the rightmost marker remain unchanged.\n4. Apply the rule to a copy of the input, preserving dimensions and every unaffected cell. Validate row widths and inspect all changed coordinates.\n\n## Evidence from a solved stream task\nTwo demos showed rows beginning with repeated markers (color 8 or 9) whose terminal suffix after the rightmost marker was recolored to 1. In one demo the suffix was background; in another it was a different color. A full-width marker row and marker-pattern rows beginning away from the left edge stayed unchanged. description: Use for ARC-style grid puzzles. Infer rules from examples.

# ARC grid reasoning

Use this skill for ARC and ARC-like grid tasks, including continual streams where each instance is independent and the response protocol is strict.

## Core workflow

1. **Read the task protocol first.** Record allowed actions, attempt/demo caps, and exact output format. For a stream protocol that requires one action JSON on the last line, emit exactly one action per turn; do not add explanation or unrelated tool output to the answer.
2. **Inventory the grid.** Note dimensions, background color, non-background colors, connected components, repeated shapes, symmetry, and isolated markers. Distinguish the likely source object/template from the objects that indicate where or how to apply it.
3. **Extract rules from every demonstration.** Compare input and output cell-by-cell. Track what stays fixed, what changes, what is removed, and what is added. Test whether changes are local to markers, aligned to object bounds, or global. Prefer a compact rule that explains all examples, not just one visually salient feature.
4. **Resolve anchor and orientation explicitly.** For any copied or expanded pattern, determine whether the marker denotes the top-left, center, endpoint, or another anchor. Check rotations/reflections, direction, offsets, boundary clipping, and overlap behavior against demonstrations. Do not assume a component is copied around every marker merely because its shape looks like a template.
5. **Use demos strategically.** Request another example only when there is a concrete unresolved distinction between plausible rules and the expected information could change the answer. After receiving one, analyze it before requesting another. Avoid repeated requests made without extracting the information already supplied; each request has a cost.
6. **Construct and validate the candidate.** Preserve dimensions unless examples establish otherwise. Build the result systematically, then check every modified cell against the inferred rule, preserve all unaffected cells, verify row widths/heights and palette, and inspect overlaps and edges. For generated grids, prefer a small script or explicit coordinate transforms over manual copying, then inspect the complete serialized grid.
7. **Submit only when the rule is adequately supported.** If there is a correctness response, use it to update the hypothesis rather than repeating the same transformation. A wrong submission is evidence that some assumption—often anchor, direction, overwrite semantics, or which object is the template—was wrong.

## Aligned-panel nonzero overlap (validated task-04691f01)
When a full uniform row or column separates two equally sized aligned panels, produce a single panel with color 2 exactly at coordinates where both corresponding input cells are nonzero; output 0 everywhere else. The task has a persistent 10x15 vertical-divider variant: a full color-8 column at c=7 leaves 10x7 panels, with a sparse color-6 marker field on the left and sparse color-4 markers on the right (background 0). Output is 10x7 with 2 iff both aligned panel cells are nonzero. This recurrence's accepted output had exactly three 2s at output coordinates (r,c)=(4,5),(5,6),(7,6), all other cells 0. Another task-04691f01 demo had a full color-9 horizontal divider: the upper 7x27 panel was mostly 8 with sparse 0s, and the lower panel contained 0s and sparse 7s. The 7x27 output had 2 exactly where upper!=0 AND lower!=0 (equivalently, upper=8 and lower=7 in that demo). In the test, a full color-6 divider separated 3x27 panels, the upper panel was mostly 1 with sparse 0s and the lower mostly 9 with sparse 0s; the correct result was 2 where upper=1 AND lower=9, and 0 otherwise. The lower panel's nonzero field color may vary; do not assume a particular palette or rely on dominant-color matching without checking the nonzero-overlap rule. Preserve aligned coordinates and discard the divider and source panels. This rule is also consistent with other aligned-panel marker/field examples; verify the exact predicate from each demo.

## Repeated stencil in a noisy grid

Some tasks use a small colored seed object as a stencil: find every translated location where each seed-colored footprint cell falls on the grid's designated target color, then recolor those footprint cells with the seed color. **Do not assume the target is the most common/background-looking color**: infer it from demonstrations by testing exact matches of the seed's occupied footprint against each plausible color and comparing the resulting changes cell-by-cell. In a demonstrated case, the target was color 0 even though the noisy field's dominant color was 3 (and another demo's dominant field color was 8); matching the majority color produced many false placements, while exact color-0 matches explained every output change. Check only the seed's occupied cells: holes in its bounding box may contain arbitrary noise and do not constrain a match. The rest of the grid—including other noise/background-looking colors—stays unchanged. Infer the stencil from the seed's color cells within its bounding box, preserving holes and disconnected cells; do not fill its full rectangle unless the seed occupies it. Validate by checking every occupied footprint cell at each candidate, then union placements (overlaps are harmless when they use the same color). This pattern is demonstrated by examples with random noise and sparse, non-rectangular seeds. A confirmed variant uses a 3×3 color-5 seed with occupied offsets {(0,2),(1,1),(1,2),(2,0),(2,2)}; color-4 noise fills much of the grid, but valid translated stencil locations are exactly those where all five occupied offsets are color 0. Overlay color 5 on those five cells, preserve the other cells (including the stencil's holes), and allow matches to overlap.

## Line-directed object translation with a trailing highlight

A recurring pattern is a full straight line in one color and a separate compact object elsewhere, both oriented so the object can move toward the line along the perpendicular axis. Demonstrations may show the object translated until it is directly adjacent to the line, with a strip in a third color (observed color 8) placed immediately on the object's far side, opposite the line. The strip matches the object's cross-section: a 1×N object produces a 1×N strip, while an M×N rectangle may produce an M×1 strip. Verify which object moves, that the full line remains unchanged, the direction and adjacency, and the exact trail location/width from demos before applying. Preserve the object's shape and colors. For a test case, move the smaller separated object toward the complete line until it touches, then place the demonstrated highlight strip just beyond it on the away-from-line side; leave all else unchanged.

## Hypothesis discipline

- Maintain a short list of candidate rules and the observation each predicts. Eliminate candidates using exact coordinates from all demos.
- Separate *what* is transformed (markers, components, rows/columns, background regions) from *how* it is transformed (copy, recolor, extend, tile, rotate, connect).
- Avoid anchoring on one example or a familiar ARC motif. Verify the rule against a second independent arrangement whenever available.
- Do not treat an unsuccessful guess as a validated procedure. Record uncertainty and gather discriminating evidence before spending a submission.
- When examples contain an object that could be either a stencil or an ordinary instance, test whether its non-background cells encode the same rule as the scattered elements; do not infer replication solely from proximity.

## Recoloring by repeated silhouettes (candidate rule; verify exact deltas)

When a grid contains a large line/corner-like component plus several scattered colored components, and demonstrations recolor exactly one component, test whether the recolored component's silhouette is congruent (translation, rotation, or reflection) to a component of another color. Enumerate 4-connected components, normalize their occupied-cell coordinates to their bounding-box origin, and compare exact sets under the 8 square symmetries. Use input/output cell diffs to identify the target component and the replacement color; in several examples the target matched a differently colored component while being recolored to the color of a prominent structural marker. Treat this as a candidate rule, not a guarantee.

Do not assume that any matching component is the target: demonstrations can contain repeated singleton or repeated-shape distractors, and some cases may select only one based on its relation to the prominent line/frame. If multiple congruent candidates exist, use another demo to resolve the selection predicate. If no whole-component match exists, do not improvise by recoloring the closest-looking component or a matching subpattern; investigate partial matching, connectivity convention, or a different rule. After an incorrect submission, re-derive the exact changed cells from all demos and request a discriminating example rather than cycling through nearby guesses. Preserve all non-target cells.

## Stream-task response discipline

In benchmark conversations that require an action object, the final line must contain exactly one valid action object and no additional action. Use the task's given grid dimensions and integer palette exactly. If asking for a demo, do not also submit a grid in that turn. If the instance is not over, do not use a finish action unless the protocol permits it.

## Left-anchored partial-row tail recoloring (validated task-0667a4e0)

A horizontal row may contain a solid run of one non-background color anchored at the left edge, followed by a contiguous background-color suffix. Recolor that suffix to color 1, preserving the left run and all other rows. A demonstrated 27×16 case changed row 5 (0-indexed): eight leading 4s stayed, and the eight following 0s became 1s; a separate full-width row of 4s stayed unchanged because it had no background suffix. In one solved test, row 12 had eleven leading 2s followed by five 7s; only the five-cell suffix became 1, while a full row of 2s stayed unchanged. A fresh 22×25 recurrence confirmed the same selection: row 16 had twenty leading 9s followed by five 0s, and only those five trailing 0s became 1; a separate full-width row of 9s stayed unchanged. These cases support selecting the incomplete left-anchored uniform row and changing its right suffix, independent of the leading marker and background colors. Preserve dimensions and every unrelated cell. Use a demo if a future variant has multiple partial rows, internal interruptions, or ambiguous candidate rows; do not generalize this evidence to materially different structures without checking.

**Caution for task-0667a4e0 recurrence:** Later instances under this task id differed substantially. One 12×27 case had repeated 2-row color-5 patterns in a color-8 field and eight demos; repeated suffix-to-1 hypotheses failed in all eight attempts. Some demos did show row-tail recoloring after a long full-color run, but many superficially similar tails were unchanged, so a generic last-marker/right-tail rule was not established. Treat the task ID as potentially multiple variants; do not reuse either the simple left-prefix rule or the failing broad tail guesses without exact demo-delta validation. After a failed submission, materially revise the selector and compare candidate changes against unchanged near-matches. In the 12×27 failure, rows were 2-row motifs with sparse 5 markers and alternating 5/8 segments; despite the apparent repeating patterns, no inferred continuation was validated. Preserve this as an unresolved caution, not a solution.

## Fixed-orientation L-triomino stencil in a noisy field (validated instance)

A sparse color-7 L triomino with occupied offsets `[(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)]` can serve as a stencil over scattered color-0 cells in a mostly color-9 field. In the solved instance, every translated occurrence of those exact three offsets where all three cells were 0 was recolored to 7, and all other cells—including additional 0s connected to the matches—were preserved. The marker's orientation mattered: search only the same orientation unless demonstrations establish rotations/reflections. Apply matches cellwise, allowing overlaps; do not recolor an entire connected component or all zeros in a matching component. Verify by enumerating each candidate origin and its three cells against the input before overlaying the color. This is evidence from one solved instance; confirm the predicate with demos if future instances differ in marker shape, color roles, or output behavior.

## Four-quadrant rotational tiling (validated task-dbd9720f)
When the input grid is square, task-dbd9720f transforms it into a 2H×2W canvas of four rotational copies: upper-left is the original input, upper-right is a 90° clockwise rotation, lower-left is a 90° counterclockwise rotation, and lower-right is a 180° rotation. Preserve every cell/color. Construct by block concatenation: `[[G, rotate_cw(G)], [rotate_ccw(G), rotate_180(G)]]`. This rule was supported by three demos (15×15, 13×13, 5×5), a correct 13×13 test submission, and a correct 4×4 test submission; the latter produced an 8×8 output. Thus, the concatenated result is 2H×2W. For non-square inputs, verify output dimensions/orientation from demos before assuming the same arrangement.

### Continual recurrence: task-dbd9720f
The four-rotation tiling rule also solved a fresh 11×11 test with zero wrong attempts, producing a 22×22 output. This provides independent recurrence evidence that the arrangement is UL=original, UR=90° clockwise, LL=90° counterclockwise, LR=180° rotation, by concatenating the rotated grids as blocks. Compute rotations mechanically and validate 2H×2W dimensions before submission.

A fresh 8×8 recurrence was also submitted correctly with zero wrong attempts; the expected output was 16×16. This further supports applying the four-rotation block rule to small square inputs, including asymmetric/noisy grids with no apparent panel markers. Mechanically construct all three rotations and concatenate the four blocks; verify output is 2H×2W and preserve each original cell exactly once per rotated copy. A completely uniform 11×11 grid (all color 5) also yielded a correct 22×22 all-5 output under the same rule; uniformity does not change the doubled-canvas output size or require a special case.

The top-left panel's complete 3×6 contents (including color-1 background) were copied into all six panels at identical local offsets; preserve divider rows/column. Infer boundaries and panel sizes first, then check alignment. Treat source-panel selection and whether to copy only occupied cells or the full tile as hypotheses unless demos support them.
